title: Palace: Duterte arrest, ICC turnover in line with Philippines laws
summary: The arrest and transfer of former president Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague was not about sovereignty and was in line with existing laws, Malacañang said yesterday.

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — The arrest and transfer of former president Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague was not about sovereignty and was in line with existing laws, Malacañang said yesterday.

Palace press officer Claire Castro said Republic Act 9851 enacted in 2009 allows the surrendering of someone accused of crimes against humanity to international bodies, adding that the Supreme Court has ruled that the International Criminal Court has jurisdiction over any crime or act committed before the country’s withdrawal from the ICC.
The Duterte family earlier expressed disappointment over the high court’s decision to junk the petitions questioning the apprehension.

“If we accepted RA 9851 and we are a former member of the ICC, we are not talking about sovereignty because we ourselves became a voluntary member and we created the RA 9851,” Castro said in a media briefing in Baguio City yesterday.

Duterte was apprehended on an ICC warrant on March 11, 2025 for alleged crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on illegal drugs. He is now detained in The Hague and is set to face trial next week.

His children, Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte, Mayor Sebastian Duterte and Veronica, had filed petitions for habeas corpus before the Supreme Court, questioning the legality of his arrest and arguing that the Philippines is no longer a member of the ICC.
The former president withdrew the Philippines from the Rome Statute, the treaty that formed the ICC, in 2019.

The high court has dismissed the petitions, saying a writ of habeas corpus is a domestic remedy enforceable only within the Philippines. Since Duterte is now under ICC custody in The Hague, Philippine courts cannot enforce a writ affecting his detention or release, it added.

The high court added that the argument stating that the arrest was invalid because of the Philippines’ withdrawal from the Rome Statute “must be pursued through the appropriate legal proceedings rather than through a petition for habeas corpus.”

On Wednesday, Paolo Panelo, counsel for Veronica, said his client would file a motion for reconsideration, arguing that the decision “effectively reduces the great writ of habeas corpus to a race to remove the person detained outside Philippine territory before the courts can act.”
In a statement, Duterte’s eldest daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte said no foreign court or nation should ever stand above the sovereignty of the Philippines.

“The protection of the life, liberty and fundamental rights of every Filipino citizen must remain paramount. No Philippine court should lightly dismiss a petition as moot, when the underlying issues concern national sovereignty, constitutional accountability and the government’s duty to protect the life and liberty of every Filipino from foreign interference,” the Vice President said.
Defense: No crimes against humanity

Ahead of the start of his trial next week, the defense team of the former president disputed the crimes against humanity charges filed before the ICC, saying the charges should have been tried in the Philippines.

“The case the prosecution has framed against Mr. Duterte is not a crimes against humanity case because the evidence, even taken at its highest, cannot establish the contextual elements,” defense lawyer Peter Haynes said in a 77-page pre-trial filing released on Thursday.

“There was no widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population of the Philippines. There was no State or organizational policy to murder. This is not a crimes against humanity case and, as such, does not belong before this Court,” Haynes added.

The filing, which outlined the defense’s position on the charges, presented Duterte as a leader who has implemented programs aimed at resolving social problems faced by Filipinos, including illegal drugs.

“No sensible analysis of Mr. Duterte’s policy initiatives and achievements in government could possibly conclude that he was attacking ‘the civilian population in the Philippines’,” the defense said in trying to establish the political nature of the case, including his arrest and turnover to the ICC in 2025.
It noted how the Marcos administration changed its position regarding the case after President Marcos’ alliance with the Vice President fell apart.

The defense maintained that Duterte does not bear individual criminal responsibility for the crimes alleged and that this should have been tried in the Philippines instead of bringing it before the international tribunal.

“The Philippines has a functioning criminal justice system, through which killings committed during the campaign against illegal drugs have been prosecuted and continue to be prosecuted as ordinary murders,” the defense claimed, citing the civilian-led Truth Commission and other domestic mechanisms.
The Truth Commission, which was able to identify over 8,000 victims, supports the proceedings at the ICC.
Earlier this week, Human Rights Watch (HRW) reported how Philippine authorities under Marcos failed to investigate extrajudicial killings during Duterte’s drug war.
Despite thousands of reported incidents, only five cases involving nine police officers have resulted in convictions.
Only four cases identified by a Department of Justice task force created in 2024 advanced to trial, while another three are currently under preliminary investigation.

“President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, HRW Southeast Asia researcher. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.”
